strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Distinguishing benchmark overlap at three distinct tiers (semantic question similarity, cross-model performance correlation, and capacity/perplexity signatures) is an insightful framing for meta-evaluation in LLM benchmarking.

Important empirical critique of standard benchmark agreement studies: The paper convincingly highlights how raw performance correlations across models can be heavily confounded by benchmark-orthogonal factors like question format (e.g., Multiple Choice vs. True/False) and benchmark family artifacts rather than actual measured capabilities.
Extensive experimental scope: Evaluates 32 diverse open-weight models across 88 benchmarks and subtasks, leveraging a massive corpus (RedPajama) to probe model perplexity distributions.
weaknesses: Small sample size ($m=32$) relative to feature space: Selecting features from millions of candidate tokens using $m=32$ data points poses severe statistical challenges. With $n=32$, screening $1.69 \times 10^7$ candidate tokens and running forward stepwise selection with AIC creates a high risk of selecting spuriously correlated features. It is also unclear whether the leave-one-out cross-validation re-ran the entire feature screening and forward selection pipeline inside each fold to prevent data leakage.

Cross-tokenizer comparability issues: The 32 models evaluated span disparate tokenizer vocabularies (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Qwen, GPT-2, Mistral). Perplexities and subword segmentations differ substantially across tokenizers. In Section B and E.1, the authors note splitting text on whitespace and evaluating the 'last token's perplexity', but whitespace pieces map to different subword token counts and boundaries depending on the model's tokenizer. The paper does not explain how token alignment and cross-tokenizer perplexity scale discrepancies were standardized beyond within-model z-scoring.

Flawed semantic overlap baseline: In Algorithm 3, the semantic similarity between two benchmarks is computed by concatenating all questions, truncating them to the sentence encoder's maximum sequence length $\ell$ (typically 512 tokens for MPNet), and taking the cosine similarity. Truncating concatenated questions discards the vast majority of questions in each benchmark. A standard approach (e.g., computing question-level embeddings and measuring average maximum similarity, Earth Mover's Distance, or mean pooling across question embeddings) would be far more principled and might explain why the semantic baseline performed unnaturally flat across categories.

Lack of qualitative analysis or inspection of extracted signatures: The core artifact of the paper is the 'benchmark signature' (a set of ~30 salient tokens/contexts per benchmark), yet the paper provides virtually no concrete qualitative examples of what these selected tokens actually look like. Demonstrating whether the selected tokens represent domain-specific concepts, syntactic structures, or uninterpretable statistical artifacts is essential to validating the core hypothesis.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely meta-evaluation problem in NLP/AI: understanding redundancy, overlap, and confounding factors across widely used LLM benchmarks.

The conceptual framing of examining benchmark overlap across three distinct levels—semantic similarity, performance correlation, and training corpus perplexity signatures—is thoughtful and interesting.

The empirical observation that standard performance-level benchmark agreements are heavily confounded by superficial factors (such as question format and benchmark family) is a relevant finding for the evaluation community.
The study evaluates a wide range of models (32 LLMs) across 88 benchmarks and subtasks.
weaknesses: Severe risk of overfitting and spurious correlations in feature selection: Mining 30 predictive features from $d \approx 1.69 \times 10^7$ candidate tokens with only $m=32$ data points (models) is an extreme $d \gg m$ regime. Even after correlation screening to the top/bottom 1% (which leaves over 300,000 candidate tokens), running greedy forward stepwise AIC selection on 32 samples will almost certainly fit noise (Freedman's paradox).

Likely data leakage in the cross-validation evaluation: The leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) in Section 3.2 describes holding out one model to fit the regression, but there is no indication that the massive pre-filtering and forward selection were re-executed inside each fold. If feature selection was performed globally on all 32 models before LOOCV, the reported MAE reduction (from 0.180 to 0.075) is subject to selection bias.

Unaddressed tokenizer discrepancies across models: The 32 evaluated models span diverse architectures and vocabularies (e.g., Llama-3 with 128k BPE, Gemma with 256k, GPT-2 with 50k, Qwen, OLMo). A whitespace-delimited word splits into completely different numbers and types of subword tokens across these tokenizers. Measuring the 'last token perplexity' without an explicit cross-tokenizer alignment mechanism introduces significant measurement inconsistency.

Lack of qualitative analysis and inspection of mined signatures: Despite defining 'benchmark signatures' as collections of ~30 salient tokens/contexts that supposedly represent model capacities, the manuscript does not showcase or analyze any extracted tokens for any benchmark. Without qualitative inspection, it is impossible to determine whether the selected tokens capture genuine task capabilities or arbitrary artifacts.

Potential measurement attenuation in signature overlap: Signature overlap is computed as the Spearman correlation between two 32-dimensional vectors representing model-averaged z-scored perplexities on ~30 tokens. Because these signatures are selected from noisy high-dimensional fits, the universally low correlations observed (typically < 0.3) could simply be the result of regression attenuation and noise rather than a calibrated measure of capacity overlap.

strengths: Important and timely problem: Characterizing benchmark redundancy, overlap, and the true capability space of LLMs is a crucial topic as the number of LLM benchmarks proliferates rapidly.
Interesting conceptual angle: Connecting benchmark performance to token-level perplexity on in-the-wild pretraining distributions (RedPajama) bridges training data exposure and downstream evaluation.

Compelling critique of performance-based benchmark agreement: The paper convincingly points out that raw performance correlations (e.g., in Benchmark Agreement Testing) are often confounded by surface factors such as question format (MCQ vs. True/False) and benchmark suite family.
weaknesses: Severe methodological flaw in semantic-level baseline (Algorithm 3): In lines 10–12 and 17–19 of Algorithm 3, all questions in a benchmark are concatenated together and then truncated to the maximum sequence length of the sentence transformer (ℓ, which is typically 384–512 tokens for MPNet). This means that only the first few questions of any benchmark are ever embedded, discarding the vast majority of the benchmark content. This invalidates the comparison and explains why semantic overlap was artificially restricted to a narrow range.

High risk of overfitting and selection bias (Freedman's Paradox): The study uses only m = 32 language models as data points. From ~3.38 × 10^5 screened candidate tokens (top/bottom 1% of 1.69 × 10^7), forward stepwise AIC selection selects ~30 features. Fitting ~30 features on 32 observations leaves virtually no degrees of freedom (df ≈ 2). Furthermore, it is unclear whether the reported leave-one-out cross-validation re-ran the full screening and forward selection pipeline from scratch on the 31 training models; if feature selection was performed on all 32 models prior to LOOCV, the reported MAE (0.075) suffers from severe selection leakage.

Unresolved paradox regarding format bias removal: Benchmark performance vectors y_{:, j} are admitted to be heavily confounded by question format and benchmark family. Yet the signature tokens are selected purely by linear regression to predict y_{:, j}. If the supervision target itself is dominated by format bias, the paper provides no mathematical or mechanistic explanation for how the fitted linear model would selectively discard format-predictive features in favor of pure capability features.

Complete lack of qualitative analysis or concrete examples of discovered signatures: The paper defines signatures as specific salient tokens with their preceding context, yet never displays what these tokens actually are. Presenting examples across domains (e.g., math, coding, logic) is essential to verify whether the selected tokens capture meaningful linguistic/conceptual capabilities or spurious statistical artifacts.

Presentation and execution issues: Several typos and inconsistencies exist in the text (e.g., 'llm-evalution-harness', calling panel (b) instead of (c) in Section 4.2, 'Concate()', and unexplained operations such as shuffling candidate features before deterministic forward selection in Algorithm 4, line 7).

strengths: Original and thought-provoking perspective: Grounding benchmark characterization and overlap in token-level perplexity profiles over in-the-wild pretraining corpora offers a novel angle on meta-evaluation beyond simple surface semantics and accuracy correlations.
Extensive experimental scope: Evaluates 32 diverse language models across 89 benchmarks/subtasks from MMLU, BBH, IFEval, MBPP, and AbsenceBench.

Insightful diagnostic results: Effectively demonstrates that traditional performance-level benchmark correlations are heavily confounded by superficial factors such as benchmark family and question format (e.g., MCQ vs. True/False), whereas perplexity-derived signatures are robust to these artifacts.

Thorough robustness and ablation studies: The appendix provides rigorous validation including leave-one-out cross-validation, held-out model evaluation, cross-task transfer, alternative regularization techniques (Lasso, ElasticNet), token granularity comparisons, and cross-corpus replication (RedPajama vs. Dolma).
weaknesses: Small sample size for high-dimensional feature selection: The regression and screening pipeline selects features across millions of tokens using only $m=32$ model observations. While the authors motivate this via Sure Independence Screening (SIS) and provide LOOCV validations, the regime $m=32 \ll d$ carries inherent susceptibility to spurious correlations.

Questionable implementation of the semantic-level overlap baseline: Algorithm 3 indicates that benchmark questions are concatenated and truncated to the maximum input length $\ell$ of the sentence transformer (typically 384 or 512 tokens for MPNet). For larger benchmarks, this discards the vast majority of questions, making the semantic similarity metric heavily truncated and potentially explaining why semantic overlap scores are uniformly narrow.

Limited interpretability of extracted signature tokens: As shown in Appendix A.9, several high-predictive tokens appear disconnected from the target domain (e.g., an excerpt from Poe's *The Raven* serving as a salient signature for coding). While the authors acknowledge this phenomenon in Section 5, the explanations remain largely speculative regarding what specific capabilities or artifacts these non-domain tokens actually capture.

strengths: Original and interesting perspective: The paper introduces the concept of 'benchmark signatures' using token-level perplexity over in-the-wild corpora to profile benchmarks, offering a novel alternative to surface-level semantic similarity and raw performance correlation.

Important diagnosis of benchmark agreement testing: The paper convincingly demonstrates that standard performance-level correlations are heavily confounded by benchmark-orthogonal factors, such as question format (e.g., MCQ vs. True-False) and benchmark suite family.
Comprehensive empirical scope: The meta-evaluation investigates 32 open-weight models across 89 benchmarks/subtasks, evaluating both RedPajama and Dolma corpora.

Extensive robustness and sensitivity analysis in the appendix: The authors provide thorough ablations on token granularity (token vs. chunk vs. doc), screening methods (Thrush vs. Spearman vs. Mutual Information), regularization techniques (AIC forward selection vs. Lasso vs. ElasticNet), cross-corpus stability (0.895 correlation between RedPajama and Dolma), and out-of-sample model generalization via LOOCV.
weaknesses: Risk of spurious correlations due to small sample size ($m=32$): Performing forward variable selection over millions of candidate token features with only 32 data points (models) is statistically susceptible to false discoveries. While the authors argue for Sure Independence Screening (SIS) conditions and report LOOCV, $m=32$ models that share overlapping lineages (e.g., multiple Llama, Qwen, and Phi checkpoints) provide very limited effective degrees of freedom.

Lack of semantic interpretability of extracted signatures: As highlighted in Section 5 and Appendix A.9, many selected tokens appear largely disconnected from the task domain (e.g., an excerpt from Poe's Raven predicting 'Coding', or Malaysian printing services predicting 'Instruction Following'). While the authors speculate about proxy cues and auxiliary demands, this weakens the claim that signatures reflect domain-specific capability demands rather than idiosyncratic proxies of model scaling.

Conceptual tension regarding format de-biasing: Benchmark performance vectors $y_{:,j}$ are used directly as regression targets during feature selection. If $y_{:,j}$ inherently contains format-specific artifacts (as shown in Figure 4b), it remains theoretically puzzling why linear feature selection on token perplexities would filter out these format biases rather than fitting them. A clearer theoretical or empirical explanation for this regularizing effect is needed.

Writing polish and presentation defects: The abstract ends with an incomplete, cut-off sentence ('We have open-sourced the code and data in this'). Additionally, there are minor typos such as 'silent tokens' instead of 'salient tokens' (Section 5, page 10) and 'llm-evalution-harness' (Appendix A.5).

strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: As the LLM community faces benchmark saturation and redundancy, analyzing benchmark overlap beyond surface semantics and raw performance correlation is a highly important and relevant research direction.
Broad experimental scale: The study evaluates 32 diverse language models across 89 benchmarks/subfields and scans billions of tokens across large-scale pretraining corpora (RedPajama and Dolma).

Extensive robustness and sensitivity investigations in the appendix: The authors provide detailed ablation studies, including comparisons across regularizers (AIC, Lasso, Elastic Net), feature screening metrics (Thrush, Spearman, Mutual Information), cross-corpus stability (RedPajama vs. Dolma), and token downsampling thresholds.

Insightful critique of performance-level correlation: The paper provides concrete evidence showing that standard performance rank correlations are heavily confounded by superficial factors such as evaluation format (e.g., True/False vs. Multiple Choice) and benchmark family groupings.
weaknesses: Severe risk of overparameterization in feature selection: The regression setup operates with only $m = 32$ observations (models) against a massive feature space ($d' \approx 1.69 \times 10^7$ candidate tokens). The stepwise forward selection terminates with approximately ~30 features per benchmark. Fitting an OLS model with ~30 parameters on 32 data points leaves almost no residual degrees of freedom ($N - p \approx 2$), which almost guarantees near-perfect collinearity/fit regardless of true underlying signal, casting substantial doubt on standard AIC termination.

Potential data leakage in validation: In Appendix A.7.1, the LOOCV reports an MAE of 0.076. It is unclear whether the entire two-stage feature selection pipeline (screening and forward AIC selection) was re-executed strictly within each cross-validation fold, or if features were selected once on the full 32-model dataset and subsequently evaluated. If the latter, the reported cross-validation results suffer from significant feature selection leakage.

Interpretability and semantic dissonance of extracted tokens: The qualitative analysis (Section 5 and Appendix A.9) reveals that the extracted signature tokens often appear completely arbitrary and detached from the benchmark's intended skill (e.g., the coding signature token is the token 'evil' from an analysis of Edgar Allan Poe's Raven; the math signature token is 'price' in an macroeconomics snippet). This strongly indicates that the signatures may capture idiosyncratic loss characteristics or noise across the 32 models rather than genuine capability fingerprints.

Conflation with general model scaling and capability: Model perplexity across large corpora and benchmark accuracy are both monotonic functions of model capability and compute scaling. While within-model z-scoring helps normalize absolute loss scales, it does not fully disentangle whether the correlations between benchmark performance and token perplexity reflect specific capability overlap or simply residual model-family/scale effects.

 Figure 1: ...'). In addition, key heatmaps and correlation plots (Figure 1 and Figure 4) are difficult to read due to overly small fonts and dense labels.
